extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literature, classicists, and creative writers studying myth and mythic characterization
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for portraying mythic/divine characters (especially Dionysus/Greek gods) in art and literature by using natural forces, sensory detail, ritual, duality, and metamorphosis to create depth and cultural grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment of natural forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict gods as personifications of natural phenomena (e.g., Zeus as the open sky; Dionysus as fire-born and dew-born).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the primary, physical signification of a deity to determine artistic expression: e.g., Pheidias 'shed... the blandness, the breadth, the smile of the open sky' upon Zeus of Olympia. Let thunder, rain, wind, sun, dew, etc., inform posture, expression, and aura so worshippers/readers feel the physical quality the god represents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condense impressions of nature into human form
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination should 'condense the impressions of natural things into human form,' retaining the 'mystical sense of water, or wind, or light' in facial and bodily expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate sensory and environmental qualities (light, wind, water) into specific features—eye, brow, hair, movement—so the human figure embodies those natural impressions rather than merely illustrating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance human form with the floating essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a tension between the 'palpable and limited human form' and the 'floating essence' it is meant to contain; avoid losing the mystical element through over-humanisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of the struggle between a definite human depiction and the need to imply wider, often indistinct cosmic forces. The Dorian tendency toward clear human form risks suppressing the 'free spirit'—retain suggestive, elusive qualities even in realistic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rich sensory, localized detail to evoke place
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ sounds, sights, smells, and tactile impressions of specific locales (wells, vineyards, city water pipes, cries of 'Acqua fresca!') to create a vivid, poetic setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, precise sensory details (darkness of a well, the ring of ferns, the sound of water through wooden pipes) anchor mythic themes in lived experience and make the atmosphere communicative and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage names as condensed associative instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mythic names (Helen, Dionysus, etc.) as summary instruments that bring with them trains of association and complex impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use names as shorthand to evoke wide experiential and cultural baggage; a single name can summon 'a hundred associations'—so select and deploy names to carry layered meaning rather than only denotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ dualities and ambivalence for depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray gods and mythic figures as twofold—e.g., Dionysus as both summer and winter, joyful and suffering—to create tragic depth and moral ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make dual aspects central to characterization (birth/death, joy/melancholy, rural/urban). Use these tensions to generate narrative conflict and psychological complexity rather than flattening a figure into a single trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor myth in ritual and festival imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rites, festivals, and cult-practices (Oinophoria, Anthestêria, Lenaeum, Eleusinian mysteries) to situate mythic figures within cultural life and recurring ceremonial patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate processions, sacred objects, seasonal rites, and communal celebrations as structural and symbolic elements that reveal popular perceptions of the deity and provide motifs for drama and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow melancholy and suffering to generate tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that 'out of the sorrows of Dionysus... all Greek tragedy grows'—suffering and loss are fertile sources for dramatic and ethical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grief, persecution, and bodily torment (e.g., Zagreus' rending, Pentheus' fate) not merely for shock but to explore moral, spiritual, and communal responses; let suffering be formative and thematically central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metamorphosis and symbolic transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ physical transformations (maenads becoming vines, women turned into bats or moths) as emblematic devices linking humans, animals, and plants to divine action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metamorphosis serves as a poetic mechanism to externalize inner change or divine retribution and to literalize metaphors—use transformations to dramatize relationships between mortals and natural/divine forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace etiology and migratory origins to ground character
rubrics_metrics.description: Situate mythic figures in historical/geographic migrations and local cults (Dionysus from Phrygia to Thrace to Athens) to explain variations in character and worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use place-of-origin, local legends, and the history of a cult's adoption to justify and enrich differing portrayals—rural vigor vs. city refinement can be explained by cultural movement and assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve ambiguity and use fragmentary tradition creatively
rubrics_metrics.description: When sources are scattered or obscure (Orphic fragments, late allusions), 'put patiently together' hints to reconstruct a subtler portrait rather than forcing a single coherent narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fragmentary evidence as a resource: assemble evocative, suggestive reconstructions that honor gaps and contradictions, allowing mystery and interpretive space in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast rustic vigor and urbane grace to show cultural change
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict the shift from 'rough country feasts' to 'feasts of the town'—the god's image changing from ruddy vineyard-born to 'honey-pale' urbane figure—to illustrate social and aesthetic transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical appearance, manners, festival style, and artistic representation to signal cultural assimilation and its effects on a deity's character and the arts (comedy/tragedy arising from these shifts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use resurrection/second-birth symbolism for ethical or mystical themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the motif of 'second birth' or resurrection (spring awakening, Orphic regeneration) as an allegory for moral purification and the hope of spiritual renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame cycles of death and rebirth as metaphors for inner transformation; such symbols can serve a minority's mystical or ethical program within a broader popular religion, and be used to give mythic narrative a moral or soteriological dimension.
